label: The logic synthesis flow
lesson:
# The logic synthesis flow

Logic synthesis turns register-transfer-level code into a netlist of library cells that computes the same function between registers. It sits between elaboration, which produces a word-level design, and physical design, which places and routes the cells. A tool designer needs the stages and the representation each one uses, because almost every later quality problem (area, timing, congestion) traces back to a choice made here.

## From RTL to a Boolean network

Elaboration resolves parameters, generate blocks and hierarchy, leaving word-level operators (adders, comparators, multiplexers) and processes (always blocks). The front end then infers storage: every variable assigned on a clock edge becomes a flip-flop, and an incompletely assigned combinational variable becomes a latch. What remains between registers is combinational logic. Word-level operators are lowered (bit-blasted) into single-bit logic, giving a **Boolean network**: a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are Boolean functions of their fanins. In Yosys this is the path from RTLIL processes through `proc` to cells and finally to single-bit gates; in ABC the network becomes an and-inverter graph. From here on synthesis optimizes only the combinational network, with registers as its boundary.

## Technology-independent optimization, then mapping

The classic flow splits optimization in two. **Technology-independent** optimization restructures the network using a library-free cost: literal count, AIG node count, and logic depth. It runs two-level minimization of node functions, algebraic factoring and extraction, don't-care simplification, and AIG rewriting and balancing. **Technology mapping** then covers the optimized network with cells from a library (or with K-input lookup tables for FPGAs), choosing cells by area, delay and load. After mapping come sizing, buffering and local resynthesis. The split is a heuristic: the cost used before mapping is only a proxy for what the library will charge, and the mapper is biased by the structure it is handed.

## Why every stage is heuristic

Even minimizing a single two-level function is NP-hard: it contains set covering. Multi-level optimization has a vastly larger space (any circuit computing the function), so tools apply local, greedy transformations that improve a cost and preserve function. Two consequences matter for a tool designer. First, results depend on the order and mix of transformations, which is why scripts such as ABC's resyn2 exist and why agents can search over them. Second, small input changes can redirect many greedy decisions, so engineering-change flows patch an existing netlist rather than resynthesize. Correctness is never heuristic: every transformation must preserve the function, and combinational equivalence checking proves it.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), the introductory chapters; Hachtel and Somenzi, "Logic Synthesis and Verification Algorithms" (1996), the introduction; the Yosys manual's description of the synth command.

problems.q:
In which representation does a modern open-source flow do most technology-independent optimization?

A) The abstract syntax tree of the RTL

B) A two-level PLA cover of every output

C) A Liberty timing table

D) An and-inverter graph
problems.a: An and-inverter graph
problems.e: ABC represents combinational logic as an AIG and applies rewriting, refactoring, balancing and resubstitution to it.

problems.q:
In which representation does a modern open-source flow do most technology-independent optimization?

A) A Liberty timing table

B) The abstract syntax tree of the RTL

C) A two-level PLA cover of every output

D) An and-inverter graph
problems.a: An and-inverter graph
problems.e: ABC represents combinational logic as an AIG and applies rewriting, refactoring, balancing and resubstitution to it.

problems.q:
Which ordering matches the classic logic synthesis flow from RTL?

A) Place the cells, then elaborate the RTL, then optimize the netlist using wire delays

B) Map RTL directly to library cells, then elaborate the hierarchy, then optimize the Boolean network

C) Elaborate RTL to a word-level netlist, lower it to a Boolean network, optimize technology-independently, then map to library cells

D) Optimize the Boolean network first, then elaborate the RTL, then map, then lower word-level operators
problems.a: Elaborate RTL to a word-level netlist, lower it to a Boolean network, optimize technology-independently, then map to library cells
problems.e: Elaboration resolves parameters and hierarchy into a word-level netlist, which is lowered to bit-level logic, optimized without a library, and finally covered with library cells.

problems.q:
Which quantity is the usual technology-independent proxy for delay?

A) The number of logic levels (depth) of the network

B) The total literal count of the network

C) The number of primary outputs

D) The number of distinct variables in the support of each output
problems.a: The number of logic levels (depth) of the network
problems.e: Depth counts gates on the longest path, so it tracks delay before cells and wires are known; literal count tracks area.

problems.q:
Which quantity is the usual technology-independent proxy for delay?

A) The number of primary outputs

B) The number of logic levels (depth) of the network

C) The total literal count of the network

D) The number of distinct variables in the support of each output
problems.a: The number of logic levels (depth) of the network
problems.e: Depth counts gates on the longest path, so it tracks delay before cells and wires are known; literal count tracks area.

problems.q:
Why is exact minimization of a multi-level network not attempted in practice?

A) Multi-level networks have no well-defined cost function

B) Even two-level minimization is NP-hard, and the multi-level search space is far larger

C) Exact minimization would change the function of the circuit

D) Exact methods exist but produce larger circuits
problems.a: Even two-level minimization is NP-hard, and the multi-level search space is far larger
problems.e: Minimum two-level cover is already a set-covering problem; multi-level optimization is attacked with heuristics that improve a cost locally.

problems.q:
Placement later finds that a synthesized net has a fanout of 400 and a long wire. Which synthesis decision most likely caused it?

A) Elaboration flattened the hierarchy, which doubles fanout

B) Technology-independent sharing extracted a common subexpression without any notion of physical distance

C) State encoding chose one-hot, which always creates large fanout

D) The mapper refused to use buffers because they have no function
problems.a: Technology-independent sharing extracted a common subexpression without any notion of physical distance
problems.e: Sharing minimizes literals but can create high-fanout nets whose sinks are spread across the die; physical synthesis and buffering must repair them.

A) Technology-independent sharing extracted a common subexpression without any notion of physical distance

B) The mapper refused to use buffers because they have no function

C) State encoding chose one-hot, which always creates large fanout

D) Elaboration flattened the hierarchy, which doubles fanout
problems.a: Technology-independent sharing extracted a common subexpression without any notion of physical distance
problems.e: Sharing minimizes literals but can create high-fanout nets whose sinks are spread across the die; physical synthesis and buffering must repair them.

problems.q:
A flow optimizes an AIG well, but the mapped netlist is poor. What is a structural reason?

A) The mapper can only choose among cuts present in the AIG's structure, so the subject graph biases the result

B) AIG optimization changes the function, which the mapper must undo

C) Library cells cannot implement functions with more than two inputs

D) Mapping ignores the AIG and reads the RTL again
problems.a: The mapper can only choose among cuts present in the AIG's structure, so the subject graph biases the result
problems.e: Structural bias is a known limitation of cut-based mapping; ABC's structural choices let the mapper see several equivalent structures at once.

label: Literal count, gate count and depth as cost
lesson:
# Literal count, gate count and depth as cost

Before a library is chosen, synthesis needs numbers to optimize. The classic ones are the literal count of a sum of products or factored form, the number of two-input gates or AIG nodes, and the logic depth. They are cheap to compute and update incrementally, and they correlate with mapped area and delay well enough to steer restructuring. Knowing exactly how each is counted is the first computational skill of the domain.

## Counting literals

A **literal** is a variable or its complement. A cube (product term) such as $a\bar{b}c$ has three literals, and the literal count of a sum of products is the total over its cubes: $f = a\bar{b}c + \bar{a}d$ has $3 + 2 = 5$ literals. Complemented and uncomplemented occurrences count the same, because in CMOS each literal is roughly one transistor pair in the gate it feeds. Literal count of a factored form counts leaf occurrences: $(a + b)(c + d)$ has 4 literals while its SOP $ac + ad + bc + bd$ has 8. This is why multi-level synthesis prefers factored-form literals as its area measure: they track the transistor count of a static CMOS implementation better than SOP literals do.

## Two-input gate count

Build an SOP with two-input AND and OR gates and free inverters. A cube with $l$ literals needs $l - 1$ ANDs, and $k$ cubes need $k - 1$ ORs. The total is $\sum_i (l_i - 1) + (k - 1) = L - 1$, where $L$ is the literal count. For $f = a\bar{b}c + \bar{a}d + bd$: $L = 7$, so 6 two-input gates (2 + 1 + 1 ANDs and 2 ORs). The same identity holds for any factored form: a form with $L$ leaves has $L - 1$ binary operators. It is the reason an AIG built from a factored form has (leaves minus one) AND nodes, and the reason literal count and two-input gate count move together.

## Depth as the delay proxy

Depth is the number of gate levels on the longest input-to-output path. Built from balanced two-input trees, a cube of $l$ literals has depth $\lceil \log_2 l \rceil$ and an OR of $k$ cubes adds $\lceil \log_2 k \rceil$, so a two-level SOP has depth $\lceil \log_2 l_{max} \rceil + \lceil \log_2 k \rceil$. For three cubes of widths 4, 3, 3 that is $2 + 2 = 4$. Depth tracks delay before cells and wires exist, but it ignores fanout load and wire length. Area and depth conflict: factoring reduces literals but can lengthen paths, and balancing reduces depth but can duplicate logic. Synthesis scripts interleave both kinds of move.

## Going deeper

Hachtel and Somenzi, "Logic Synthesis and Verification Algorithms" (1996); De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), the chapter on multiple-level optimization.

problems.q: A synthesis tool scores the cover $f = ac + \bar{b}\bar{c}d + \bar{a}b\bar{c}d$ by its literal count. How many literals does it have?
problems.e: Count every variable occurrence, complemented or not, across the 3 cubes: 9 literals.

problems.q: A synthesis tool scores the cover $f = a\bar{b}\bar{d}e + a\bar{b}e + ab\bar{d}$ by its literal count. How many literals does it have?
problems.e: Count every variable occurrence, complemented or not, across the 3 cubes: 10 literals.

problems.q: A synthesis tool scores the cover $f = b\bar{c}d + \bar{a}\bar{c}\bar{d} + \bar{a}\bar{c}d + ab + abc\bar{d}$ by its literal count. How many literals does it have?
problems.e: Count every variable occurrence, complemented or not, across the 5 cubes: 15 literals.

problems.q: Implement $f = ab + \bar{b}c + \bar{a}bcd$ as a two-level AND-OR circuit using only two-input AND and OR gates, with complemented inputs available for free. How many two-input gates are needed?
problems.e: A cube with l literals needs l - 1 two-input ANDs and 3 products need 2 two-input ORs. Total 7, which equals literals minus 1 = 8 - 1.

problems.q: Implement $f = ac\bar{d} + a\bar{d} + \bar{b}cd$ as a two-level AND-OR circuit using only two-input AND and OR gates, with complemented inputs available for free. How many two-input gates are needed?
problems.e: A cube with l literals needs l - 1 two-input ANDs and 3 products need 2 two-input ORs. Total 7, which equals literals minus 1 = 8 - 1.

problems.q: Implement $f = abcd + be + \bar{a}\bar{c}\bar{e} + bc\bar{d}\bar{e}$ as a two-level AND-OR circuit using only two-input AND and OR gates, with complemented inputs available for free. How many two-input gates are needed?
problems.e: A cube with l literals needs l - 1 two-input ANDs and 4 products need 3 two-input ORs. Total 12, which equals literals minus 1 = 13 - 1.

problems.q: Build $f = ab\bar{c}d + \bar{b}d + \bar{b}\bar{c}d + \bar{a}c$ from two-input gates, with each product and the final sum as balanced trees and complemented inputs free. What is the depth of the circuit in gate levels?
problems.e: The widest product has 4 literals, a balanced AND tree of depth 2. The sum of 4 products is an OR tree of depth 2. Depth 4.

problems.q: Build $f = ab\bar{d}\bar{e} + ae + b\bar{c}d\bar{e} + \bar{a}\bar{b}c\bar{e}$ from two-input gates, with each product and the final sum as balanced trees and complemented inputs free. What is the depth of the circuit in gate levels?
problems.e: The widest product has 4 literals, a balanced AND tree of depth 2. The sum of 4 products is an OR tree of depth 2. Depth 4.

problems.q: Build $f = bc + a\bar{b}cd + \bar{a}\bar{b}c\bar{d} + a\bar{b}c + \bar{a}\bar{d}$ from two-input gates, with each product and the final sum as balanced trees and complemented inputs free. What is the depth of the circuit in gate levels?
problems.e: The widest product has 4 literals, a balanced AND tree of depth 2. The sum of 5 products is an OR tree of depth 3. Depth 5.

label: What a synthesized netlist preserves and abstracts
lesson:
# What a synthesized netlist preserves and abstracts

A synthesized netlist is a list of library cell instances and the nets that connect them. It is the hand-off from synthesis to placement, timing and verification, so a tool designer must know exactly what it guarantees. It preserves function at registers and ports, and it discards most of what the RTL author wrote: expressions, internal names, word structure and any notion of delay.

## What the netlist guarantees

Synthesis guarantees that the netlist is **functionally equivalent** to the RTL at the registers and primary outputs: each register input and each output computes the same Boolean function of the register outputs and primary inputs. Registers and ports survive with recognizable names, so an equivalence checker can match them. Nothing else is guaranteed. Internal combinational signals can be merged, duplicated or removed; multi-bit variables are bit-blasted into single-bit nets; and an X assigned in the RTL is a don't care that synthesis resolves to whatever value simplifies the logic, which is one source of RTL versus gate-level simulation mismatches.

## What the netlist adds and what it leaves out

Mapping binds each node to a library cell, and through the cell name the netlist inherits everything the library knows: area, pin capacitances and timing arcs from Liberty, and footprint and pins from LEF. The netlist itself holds no delays and no coordinates. A timer computes delays from the netlist plus Liberty tables plus wire parasitics, and a placer assigns coordinates. This separation is deliberate: the same netlist can be timed at several corners and placed many ways. It also means synthesis decisions are made against estimates of wires that do not exist yet, which is the root of the synthesis-to-placement correlation problem.

## Consequences for verification and debug

Because only register correspondence is preserved, **combinational equivalence checking** works only when registers match one to one. Retiming breaks that correspondence and needs sequential equivalence checking. Debug taps, clock-domain-crossing synchronizers and other structures that must survive are protected with keep or dont_touch attributes, since otherwise optimization owns them. Two netlists that both pass equivalence can still differ wildly in area, timing and power: equivalence says nothing about quality. Finally, a flow that resynthesizes after a small RTL change can produce a very different netlist, so late changes are made as ECO patches that keep the rest of the netlist intact.

## Going deeper

Kuehlmann and van Eijk, "Combinational and sequential equivalence checking", in Hassoun and Sasao (eds.), "Logic Synthesis and Verification" (2002); the Liberty and LEF reference manuals for what cell views contain.

problems.q:
Which statement about an X (unknown) in RTL simulation versus the synthesized netlist is correct?

A) An X in RTL always becomes a tied-low net

B) Synthesis rejects any RTL that contains X

C) Synthesis preserves X as a third logic value in the gates

D) Synthesis may treat an X assignment as a don't care and pick any value, so the netlist can behave differently from RTL simulation
problems.a: Synthesis may treat an X assignment as a don't care and pick any value, so the netlist can behave differently from RTL simulation
problems.e: X assignments are optimization freedom for synthesis, which is one source of RTL versus gate simulation mismatch.

problems.q:
A gate-level netlist lists instances of NAND2_X1, DFF_X2 and so on with their connections. What does it preserve from the RTL?

A) The cycle-level Boolean behavior at the registers and outputs

B) The RTL's arithmetic operators as single word-level operations

C) The exact placement of each cell

D) The original always blocks and variable names, line by line
problems.a: The cycle-level Boolean behavior at the registers and outputs
problems.e: Synthesis guarantees equivalence of the combinational logic between registers (and of registered outputs), not textual structure.

problems.q:
What does a mapped netlist know about each cell that a technology-independent network does not?

A) Its fanin and fanout connections

B) Whether it is combinational or sequential

C) Its library cell type, which brings area, pin capacitance and timing arcs

D) Its Boolean function
problems.a: Its library cell type, which brings area, pin capacitance and timing arcs
problems.e: Function and connectivity exist before mapping; the library binding adds physical and timing data.

problems.q:
Two netlists are equivalence-checked against the same RTL and both pass. What does that guarantee?

A) They have identical area and timing

B) They compute the same Boolean functions at matching registers and outputs, not that they have equal timing or power

C) They are structurally identical up to renaming

D) They will both meet timing after placement
problems.a: They compute the same Boolean functions at matching registers and outputs, not that they have equal timing or power
problems.e: Equivalence is about function; QoR metrics are separate.

A) They have identical area and timing

B) They will both meet timing after placement

problems.q:
Why do flows put keep or dont_touch attributes on some nets?

A) To make synthesis run faster

B) To tell placement where to put the net

C) To force the mapper to use the largest cell

D) To stop optimization from removing or restructuring logic that must survive, such as debug taps or clock-domain-crossing structures
problems.a: To stop optimization from removing or restructuring logic that must survive, such as debug taps or clock-domain-crossing structures
problems.e: Synthesis owns everything it is allowed to change; attributes mark the exceptions.

A netlist is functionally equivalent to RTL, but the two disagree in gate-level simulation at power-up. Why can both facts be true?

A) Gate-level simulation does not model flip-flops

B) Equivalence assumes defined initial states; uninitialized registers and X-pessimism differ between the two simulations

C) Equivalence checking ignores the clock

D) The netlist must have a different number of outputs
problems.a: Equivalence assumes defined initial states; uninitialized registers and X-pessimism differ between the two simulations
problems.e: Formal equivalence is relative to state correspondence and two-valued logic; simulation X semantics can differ.

A) To force the mapper to use the largest cell

B) To make synthesis run faster

C) To stop optimization from removing or restructuring logic that must survive, such as debug taps or clock-domain-crossing structures

D) To tell placement where to put the net
problems.a: To stop optimization from removing or restructuring logic that must survive, such as debug taps or clock-domain-crossing structures
problems.e: Synthesis owns everything it is allowed to change; attributes mark the exceptions.

label: Cubes in positional notation
prereqs: Literal count, gate count and depth as cost
lesson:
# Cubes in positional notation

Two-level minimizers do not manipulate algebraic strings. They store each product term as a cube in positional notation, one symbol per variable, and implement intersection, containment, distance and consensus as bitwise operations. This is the data structure under Quine-McCluskey and Espresso, and the cube calculus is the vocabulary of every two-level algorithm that follows.

## Cubes as strings of 0, 1 and dash

Over variables $a, b, c, d$ the cube $a\bar{c}$ is written `1-0-`: position $i$ holds 1 for an uncomplemented literal, 0 for a complemented one, and a dash when the variable is absent. A cube with $k$ dashes covers $2^k$ minterms, so `1-0-` covers 4. Intersection works position by position: two specified symbols must agree, and the more specific symbol wins otherwise. `1-0-` meets `--00` in `1-00`, which covers 2 minterms; `1---` meets `0---` in the empty cube. In Espresso each position is two bits (01 for 0, 10 for 1, 11 for dash), so intersection is a bitwise AND and an empty field 00 signals an empty result.

## Distance between cubes

The **distance** between two cubes is the number of positions where one has 0 and the other has 1. Dashes never conflict. Distance 0 means the cubes intersect. For `010-` and `0-11`, position 3 has 0 against 1 and nothing else conflicts, so the distance is 1. Distance is the test behind every merge: in Quine-McCluskey two cubes with identical dash positions and distance 1 merge into one cube with a new dash. Distance 2 or more means the cubes are far apart: no single cube generated from them can cover both without other help. In Espresso the distance is computed as the number of empty fields of the bitwise AND.

## Consensus of distance-one cubes

When two cubes are at distance exactly 1, their **consensus** is formed by dropping the conflicting variable and intersecting the remaining positions. For `-00-1` and `10000` over $a$ to $e$ the conflict is in $e$; intersecting the rest gives `1000-`, a cube with 4 literals. Algebraically this is the consensus theorem $xy + \bar{x}z = xy + \bar{x}z + yz$: the consensus is implied by the two cubes together though contained in neither. Iterated consensus, with absorption of contained cubes, generates exactly the prime implicants of a cover. That is an alternative to Quine-McCluskey that starts from any cover rather than from minterms.

## Going deeper

Brayton, Hachtel, McMullen and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Logic Minimization Algorithms for VLSI Synthesis" (1984); Hachtel and Somenzi, "Logic Synthesis and Verification Algorithms" (1996), the two-level chapters.

problems.q: In positional cube notation over variables a, b, c, d, cube A is -0-0 and cube B is -111. How many minterms lie in the intersection of A and B?
problems.e: Intersect variable by variable: a 0 against a 1 makes the intersection empty, otherwise the more specific symbol wins. The result covers 0 minterms.

problems.q: In positional cube notation over variables a, b, c, d, e, cube A is 10--- and cube B is 1--0-. How many minterms lie in the intersection of A and B?
problems.e: Intersect variable by variable: a 0 against a 1 makes the intersection empty, otherwise the more specific symbol wins. The result covers 4 minterms.

problems.q: In positional cube notation over variables a, b, c, d, cube A is 1111 and cube B is 00--. How many minterms lie in the intersection of A and B?
problems.e: Intersect variable by variable: a 0 against a 1 makes the intersection empty, otherwise the more specific symbol wins. The result covers 0 minterms.

problems.q: Cubes 10-1 and 101- are written over variables a, b, c, d. What is the distance between them (the number of variables in which one has 0 and the other has 1)?
problems.e: Only positions where both cubes are specified and disagree count. There are 0. Distance 0 means they intersect; distance 1 means they have a consensus.

problems.q: Cubes -11- and -0-0 are written over variables a, b, c, d. What is the distance between them (the number of variables in which one has 0 and the other has 1)?
problems.e: Only positions where both cubes are specified and disagree count. There are 1. Distance 0 means they intersect; distance 1 means they have a consensus.

problems.q: Cubes -11-1 and 1-1-1 are written over variables a, b, c, d, e. What is the distance between them (the number of variables in which one has 0 and the other has 1)?
problems.e: Only positions where both cubes are specified and disagree count. There are 0. Distance 0 means they intersect; distance 1 means they have a consensus.

problems.q: Cubes 0-1- and 11-- (variables a, b, c, d) conflict in exactly one variable. How many literals does their consensus cube have?
problems.e: The consensus drops the conflicting variable and intersects the rest, giving -11- with 2 literals.

problems.q: Cubes -1-0 and -101 (variables a, b, c, d) conflict in exactly one variable. How many literals does their consensus cube have?
problems.e: The consensus drops the conflicting variable and intersects the rest, giving -10- with 2 literals.

problems.q: Cubes --00 and --10 (variables a, b, c, d) conflict in exactly one variable. How many literals does their consensus cube have?
problems.e: The consensus drops the conflicting variable and intersects the rest, giving ---0 with 1 literals.

label: Karnaugh-map minimization
lesson:
# Karnaugh-map minimization

A Karnaugh map lays out the truth table of a function of up to four or five variables so that logically adjacent minterms are geometrically adjacent. Grouping 1-cells into power-of-two rectangles finds implicants by eye. Synthesis tools never use maps, but the map is the cleanest picture of primes, essentials and covering, the concepts every exact and heuristic minimizer implements.

## Adjacency and implicant groups

Rows and columns are labeled in Gray-code order (00, 01, 11, 10), so neighboring cells differ in one variable, and the map wraps around at its edges. A rectangle of $2^k$ cells that are all 1 (or don't care) is an **implicant** with $n - k$ literals: the variables that stay constant across it. For $f(a,b,c,d) = \sum m(0, 4, 8, 12)$ the four cells form the column $c = 0, d = 0$, a group of 4 giving the implicant $\bar{c}\bar{d}$. Bigger groups mean fewer literals. The largest group through a minterm is the prime implicant with fewest literals that contains it, and finding it is the human version of Espresso's expand step.

## Choosing a minimum cover

A minimum sum of products uses as few product terms as possible, and among those as few literals. The procedure on a map: first take every group that is the only way to cover some 1-cell (an essential prime), then cover the remaining 1s with as few additional primes as possible. For $f = \sum m(1, 4, 5, 7, 9, 15)$ over $a, b, c, d$: minterm 9 needs $\bar{b}\bar{c}d$, minterm 4 needs $\bar{a}b\bar{c}$, and minterm 15 needs $bcd$; together they cover all six 1-cells, so the minimum has 3 products. Every product in a minimum cover can be taken prime, since enlarging a group never adds cost.

## Don't cares and the limits of maps

A don't care cell (written d or X) may be included in a group if it helps and ignored otherwise. With $f = \sum m(1, 5, 6, 11) + d(8)$ the don't care at 8 does not join any useful group, so the minimum stays $\bar{a}\bar{c}d + \bar{a}bc\bar{d} + a\bar{b}cd$ with 11 literals; in other functions one don't care can merge two pairs into a quad and save two literals. Maps stop being practical beyond five or six variables, because adjacency is no longer visible in two dimensions. The underlying problem, choosing primes to cover the ON-set, is what Quine-McCluskey and unate covering solve exactly and what Espresso solves heuristically.

## Going deeper

Karnaugh, "The map method for synthesis of combinational logic circuits", AIEE Transactions (1953); Katz and Borriello, "Contemporary Logic Design" (2nd ed.), on two-level simplification.

problems.q: On the Karnaugh map of $f(a,b,c) = \sum m(0, 2, 6, 7)$, what is the largest group of 1-cells (a power-of-two rectangle, wrapping allowed) that contains minterm 6? Give its number of cells.
problems.e: The largest implicant containing m6 covers 2 minterms; every cell of it is a 1.

problems.q: On the Karnaugh map of $f(a,b,c,d) = \sum m(1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 14)$, what is the largest group of 1-cells (a power-of-two rectangle, wrapping allowed) that contains minterm 4? Give its number of cells.
problems.e: The largest implicant containing m4 covers 4 minterms; every cell of it is a 1.

problems.q: On the Karnaugh map of $f(a,b,c,d) = \sum m(1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 14, 15)$, what is the largest group of 1-cells (a power-of-two rectangle, wrapping allowed) that contains minterm 2? Give its number of cells.
problems.e: The largest implicant containing m2 covers 2 minterms; every cell of it is a 1.

label: The Quine-McCluskey method
lesson:
# The Quine-McCluskey method

Quine-McCluskey is the tabular, exact algorithm for two-level minimization. Its first phase generates every prime implicant by repeatedly merging cubes that differ in one variable; its second phase chooses a minimum subset of primes, a covering problem. It is the textbook baseline that defines what "exact" means, and its first phase shows why exact methods blow up.

## Merging adjacent minterms

List the ON minterms (and don't cares) in binary and group them by the number of 1s. Two entries in neighboring groups that differ in exactly one bit merge into a cube with a dash in that position: 0101 and 0111 give 01-1. Only adjacent groups need to be compared, since a one-bit difference changes the count of 1s by exactly one. The number of one-dash cubes produced in this first column equals the number of pairs of adjacent ON minterms. For $\sum m(0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12)$ there are 12 such pairs, among them 0-1, 0-4, 0-8, 1-5, 1-9 and 4-5. Each entry that takes part in a merge is checked off.

## Iterating to the prime implicants

Repeat on the new column: two cubes merge if they have dashes in the same positions and differ in exactly one specified bit, producing a cube with one more dash. Duplicates (the same cube reached in two ways) are kept once. When no more merges are possible, the entries never checked off are the **prime implicants**: implicants that no larger implicant contains. For a function of $n$ variables the number of primes can grow as roughly $3^n/n$ in the worst case, and the merging tables grow with it. That growth is the reason exact two-level minimization is reserved for small functions and why Espresso never enumerates all primes.

## Don't cares and the hand-off to covering

Don't cares join the merging phase as if they were 1s, which can only enlarge primes. They do not join the covering phase: a prime that covers only don't cares is dropped, and the table has one column per ON minterm only. For $\sum m(4, 6, 7, 10, 15)$ plus don't cares, the primes that touch the ON-set become the rows of the prime implicant table. The second phase then picks a minimum set of rows covering every column. That phase is unate covering, NP-hard in general, attacked with essential-prime selection, dominance and branch and bound. Quine-McCluskey thus splits minimization into prime generation and set covering.

## Going deeper

McCluskey, "Minimization of Boolean functions", Bell System Technical Journal (1956); De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), the chapter on two-level optimization.

problems.e: Each pair of adjacent ON minterms gives one implicant with a single dash. There are 3 such pairs.

problems.q: Apply Quine-McCluskey to $f(a,b,c,d,e) = \sum m(5, 6, 8, 13, 17, 18, 19, 20, 24) + d(9, 11, 27)$, merging don't cares as if they were 1s. How many prime implicants cover at least one ON minterm (the rows of the prime implicant table)?

label: Prime implicant tables and essential primes
lesson:
# Prime implicant tables and essential primes

The second phase of exact two-level minimization works on a table: one row per prime implicant, one column per ON minterm, a mark where the prime covers the minterm. Some primes are forced into every solution because they alone cover some minterm. Finding these essential primes is the first, cheapest step of every covering algorithm, and it often solves most of the problem.

## Building the table

Take the primes from prime generation as rows and the ON minterms as columns, and mark row $p$, column $m$ when cube $p$ contains $m$. Don't-care minterms get no column, because they need not be covered. For $f = \sum m(3, 6, 8, 10, 11, 14)$ the primes are $\bar{b}cd$, $bc\bar{d}$, $ac\bar{d}$, $a\bar{b}\bar{d}$ and $a\bar{b}c$. The column for minterm 10 (1010) is marked by $ac\bar{d}$, $a\bar{b}\bar{d}$ and $a\bar{b}c$, three rows. The number of marks in a column is the number of ways that minterm can be covered, and a selection of rows is a valid cover exactly when every column has a mark in some selected row.

## Essential primes

A column with a single mark identifies an **essential prime**: that row must be in every cover. For $f = \sum m(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12)$ the primes are $\bar{b}c$, $b\bar{c}\bar{d}$, $\bar{a}c\bar{d}$, $\bar{a}b\bar{d}$ and $\bar{a}b\bar{c}$. Minterm 11 is covered only by $\bar{b}c$, minterm 12 only by $b\bar{c}\bar{d}$, and minterm 5 only by $\bar{a}b\bar{c}$, so those three are essential. Selecting an essential prime removes every column it covers. Here the three essentials cover every ON minterm except 6, which either $\bar{a}c\bar{d}$ or $\bar{a}b\bar{d}$ can cover, so the minimum has four products and two equally good completions.

## The residual problem

After removing essential rows and their columns, what remains is a smaller covering problem. If no columns remain, the essentials are the unique minimum cover. Otherwise the residue may contain new essentials (secondary essentials after dominance reductions) or may be **cyclic**: every column marked at least twice, no dominance applicable. The classic cyclic example is $f = \sum m(0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7)$ over three variables, which has six primes, none essential, and two different minimum covers of three cubes each. Cyclic cores are where branch and bound or Petrick's method are needed, and where the exponential cost of exact minimization lives.

## Going deeper

Hachtel and Somenzi, "Logic Synthesis and Verification Algorithms" (1996), on exact two-level minimization; De Micheli (1994), the chapter on two-level optimization.

label: Row and column dominance
prereqs: Prime implicant tables and essential primes
lesson:
# Row and column dominance

Between essential-prime selection and search, covering algorithms shrink the table with dominance rules. A column that is easier to satisfy than another makes the harder one redundant, and a row that covers no more than another (at no lower cost) can be dropped. Alternating these reductions with essential selection often solves the table outright and always shrinks the search.

## Essential rows in a covering table

In a general covering table, row $P_i$ covers a set of columns and every column must be covered. A row is **essential** if it is the only row marking some column. For the table $P_1 = \{c_1, c_2, c_4, c_5\}$, $P_2 = \{c_1, c_2, c_4, c_5\}$, $P_3 = \{c_5\}$, $P_4 = \{c_1, c_3\}$, $P_5 = \{c_2\}$, $P_6 = \{c_4\}$, only column $c_3$ has a single mark, so $P_4$ is the one essential row. Selecting it deletes columns $c_1$ and $c_3$, and the remaining table is smaller. Essential selection is safe: any cover must contain that row, so committing to it loses nothing.

## Column dominance

Let $R(c)$ be the set of rows that mark column $c$. If $R(c_j) \subseteq R(c_i)$, any row that covers $c_j$ also covers $c_i$, so once $c_j$ is covered $c_i$ is covered for free: delete $c_i$, the column with the larger row set. Two identical columns keep one. For example, with $R(c_1) = \{P_2, P_4\}$ and $R(c_5) = \{P_1, P_2, P_4\}$, column $c_5$ is deleted. The rule looks backwards at first: the dominating column is the one removed. Deleting columns never changes the set of valid covers, so column dominance is exact.

## Row dominance and the cyclic core

If row $P_q$'s remaining columns are a subset of row $P_p$'s and $P_p$ costs no more, then some minimum cover avoids $P_q$: replace it by $P_p$. So delete the dominated row (with unit cost, ties keep the lower index). Row dominance is safe for finding a minimum but may discard some alternative optima. Alternate essential selection, row dominance and column dominance until nothing changes. Either the table vanishes, giving the minimum cover from the selected rows, or a **cyclic core** remains in which every column is marked at least twice and no dominance applies. Only the cyclic core needs branch and bound, so these reductions decide how much search an exact minimizer must do.

## Going deeper

Coudert, "On solving covering problems", DAC 1996; Hachtel and Somenzi (1996), on unate covering reductions.

label: Unate covering
prereqs: Integer programming and branch and bound
lesson:
# Unate covering

Choosing a minimum set of primes is a unate covering problem: select rows of a 0-1 matrix so that every column is covered, at minimum cost. It is NP-hard, it appears all over EDA (test compaction, technology mapping, routing track assignment), and exact minimizers solve it with branch and bound guided by lower bounds. Writing it as an integer program makes its structure plain.

## The covering problem as an integer program

Give each row $i$ a binary variable $x_i$ (1 if selected) and a cost $w_i$. For each column $j$ add the constraint $\sum_{i \in R(j)} x_i \ge 1$: at least one row marking column $j$ is chosen. Minimize $\sum_i w_i x_i$. The constraints are **unate**: every variable appears uncomplemented, so turning a row on can never violate a constraint. A selection is feasible exactly when no column constraint is violated. For a candidate selection, counting violated constraints means counting columns none of the selected rows marks; that count is zero for a cover. The binate covering problem, which allows complemented variables, arises in state minimization and technology mapping with choices and is harder still.

## Solving by branch and bound

Exact solvers reduce the matrix (essentials, dominance), then branch: pick a column, and for each row that covers it, try including that row and recurse. A **lower bound** prunes branches: if the cost so far plus a bound on the remaining cost is no better than the best cover found, stop. A standard bound is a maximal set of pairwise disjoint columns (no row covers two of them): each needs its own row, so their count bounds the number of rows still needed. The LP relaxation, with $0 \le x_i \le 1$, gives another bound. On small tables an exhaustive search over subsets in order of size gives the minimum directly, which is how the drills here are checked.

## Costs and weighted covers

In logic minimization the row cost is usually the literal count of the prime, or one per cube when the goal is the fewest products. The two objectives can disagree: a cover with fewer cubes can have more literals. With weights the minimum is no longer the smallest set of rows. If rows cost 3, 3, 3 and 4, a two-row cover that uses the 4-cost row costs 7 while another two-row cover costs 6, and a three-row cover of cheap rows can beat a two-row cover of expensive ones. Weighted covering also changes dominance: a row can only be dropped in favor of a row that covers more and costs no more. Tools such as Espresso-exact and the covering solvers inside SIS use these weighted forms.

## Going deeper

Coudert and Madre, "New ideas for solving covering problems", DAC 1995; Hachtel and Somenzi (1996), on covering; any integer programming text on set covering.

label: Petrick's method
prereqs: Prime implicant tables and essential primes
Logical equivalence, De Morgan and normal forms
lesson:
# Petrick's method

Petrick's method solves the covering problem algebraically. Each column becomes a clause saying which rows can cover it, the product of all clauses says that every column is covered, and multiplying out with absorption lists every irredundant cover. It is exponential, but it is exact, it makes the structure of cyclic tables visible, and it is the Boolean view of what branch and bound searches.

## Writing the product of sums

Give each row (prime) a Boolean variable $P_i$, true if the row is selected. A column covered by rows $P_1$ and $P_3$ yields the clause $(P_1 + P_3)$: at least one must be selected. The covering condition is the product of all clauses, a CNF formula with only positive literals. Before expanding, simplify: duplicate clauses collapse, and a clause that contains another is implied by it and can be dropped, because $(P_1)(P_1 + P_2) = P_1$. For a table with clauses $(P_3 + P_4)$, $(P_2 + P_4)$, $(P_1 + P_4)$, $(P_1 + P_2)$ none contains another, so all four remain.

## Expanding into covers

Multiply the clauses out into a sum of products, applying $X \cdot X = X$ and absorption $X + XY = X$ as you go. Each surviving product is a set of rows that covers every column and from which no row can be removed: an **irredundant cover**. Example: $(P_1 + P_2)(P_1 + P_3)(P_2 + P_3) = (P_1 + P_2 P_3)(P_2 + P_3) = P_1 P_2 + P_1 P_3 + P_2 P_3$. There are three irredundant covers, each of two rows. Expansion can blow up exponentially in the number of clauses, so the method is practical only for small cyclic cores left after essential selection and dominance.

## Choosing the minimum

Among the products, choose the one of least cost: fewest variables for unit cost, or least total literal count when each $P_i$ is weighted by its prime's literals. Petrick's method shows every minimum at once, which reveals ties: a cyclic table such as $\sum m(0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7)$ over three variables has two different minimum covers of three primes. The expanded SOP is exactly the set of minimal transversals of the column sets, so the method also connects covering to hypergraph transversals and to the SAT view of covering, where a pseudo-Boolean or MaxSAT solver replaces hand expansion on larger cores.

## Going deeper

Petrick, "A direct determination of the irredundant forms of a Boolean function from the set of prime implicants", AFCRC technical report (1956); De Micheli (1994), the chapter on two-level optimization.

label: Tautology checking by cofactoring
lesson:
# Tautology checking by cofactoring

Most operations inside Espresso reduce to one question: is this cover a tautology, equal to 1 everywhere? Containment of a cube in a cover, redundancy of a cube, and equivalence of two covers are all tautology checks on cofactors. Espresso answers it with the unate recursive paradigm: split by Shannon cofactoring until each piece is trivially decided, using unateness to stop early.

## Cofactors of a cover

The cofactor of a cover $F$ with respect to $x = 1$ keeps every cube that does not contain $\bar{x}$ and raises $x$ in it to a dash; cubes containing $\bar{x}$ vanish. For the cover `10-`, `00-`, `-1-` over $a, b, c$, the cofactor with respect to $b = 0$ keeps `10-` and `00-` as `1--` and `0--` and drops `-1-`, leaving 2 cubes. More generally the cofactor with respect to a cube $c$ restricts the cover to the subspace of $c$. By Shannon expansion $F = x F_x + \bar{x} F_{\bar{x}}$, so $F$ is a tautology exactly when both cofactors are.

## Recursive tautology checking

Recursion splits on a variable, usually the most binate one (appearing in both polarities in the most cubes), and checks both cofactors. It stops at easy cases: a cover containing the all-dash cube is a tautology; an empty cover is not; a cover in which some column is all one polarity can be decided by unate rules; and a cover whose total minterm count is below $2^n$ cannot be a tautology. When a branch fails, the path of assignments to the failing leaf is a minterm the cover misses. Counting all uncovered minterms is a stronger question than tautology, but on small covers it can be read off the same recursion.

## Unate covers end the recursion

A cover is **unate** in a variable if that variable appears in only one polarity (or not at all). If a cover is unate in every variable, it is a tautology exactly when it contains the all-dash cube. The reason: assign each variable the value opposite to the polarity in which it appears. Every cube other than the all-dash cube has at least one literal, each such literal is now false, so the cover evaluates to 0 at that point. This is why Espresso's recursion picks binate variables to split on: each split pushes the cofactors toward unateness, where a single containment check decides them. The same paradigm computes complements and checks containment, which is what makes Espresso work on cube lists with dozens of inputs where truth tables would be impossible.

## Going deeper

Brayton et al., "Logic Minimization Algorithms for VLSI Synthesis" (1984), on the unate recursive paradigm.

label: Expanding cubes against the off-set
lesson:
# Expanding cubes against the off-set

EXPAND is the step that makes Espresso's cubes prime. It grows each cube by raising literals to dashes as long as the cube stays inside the ON-set plus don't cares, that is, as long as it does not meet the OFF-set. Bigger cubes have fewer literals and swallow other cubes of the cover, which then disappear.

## The legality test for raising a literal

Raising a literal of cube $c$ doubles it: `0011` with $a$ raised becomes `-011`, adding minterm `1011`. The move is legal only if the new cube does not intersect the OFF-set $R$, because every minterm a cube covers must be ON or don't care. Espresso keeps $R$ explicitly as a cover (computed once by complementing ON plus DC) and tests intersection cube by cube. Testing literals one at a time from the original cube tells which raises are individually possible; for `0011` with OFF minterms 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 14, raising $a$ adds 1011 (minterm 11, OFF) and fails, while raising $b$ adds 0111 (minterm 7, ON) and succeeds.

## Greedy expansion to a prime

Raising literals one after another, keeping each legal raise, ends at a cube where no further literal can be raised: a **prime implicant**. The result depends on the order. With OFF-set minterms 0, 2, 6, 9, 11, 12, 15 and the cube `1010`: raising $a$ gives `-010`, which adds minterm 2 (OFF), so it fails; raising $b$ gives `1-10`, adding 14 (ON), so keep it; raising $c$ from `1-10` gives `1--0`, adding 8 and 12, and 12 is OFF, so it fails; raising $d$ gives `1-1-`, adding 11 and 15, both OFF. The final cube is `1-10`, with 3 literals. Another order could reach a different prime.

## Steering expansion to shrink the cover

Espresso does not expand in alphabetical order. It orders literals so that the expanded cube covers as many other cubes of the current cover as possible, using a blocking matrix (which OFF cubes each raise would hit) and a covering matrix (which ON cubes the cube could absorb). Any cube fully contained in an expanded cube is deleted, so EXPAND both reduces literals and reduces the cube count. The quality of the heuristic is in that ordering: a cube expanded toward a region already covered gains nothing, while one expanded toward isolated cubes can absorb several. Cubes are processed from smallest to largest, since small cubes are the hardest to cover.

## Going deeper

Brayton et al., "Logic Minimization Algorithms for VLSI Synthesis" (1984), on EXPAND; Rudell and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Multiple-valued minimization for PLA optimization", IEEE TCAD (1987).

label: Irredundant covers
prereqs: Prime implicant tables and essential primes
lesson:
# Irredundant covers

After expansion every cube is prime, but the cover may still contain cubes that the others already cover. IRREDUNDANT removes them. It is not simply deleting every redundant cube: removing one can make another necessary. Espresso classifies the cubes and solves a small covering problem over the ones that are only partially redundant.

## Relatively essential cubes

A cube of a cover is **relatively essential** if it covers some minterm (outside the don't-care set) that no other cube of the cover covers. Such a cube must stay in every subcover. For the cover `-110`, `00-1`, `1-10`, `11-0`, `111-` of a function of $a, b, c, d$, each cube can be checked by asking whether it is contained in the union of the others plus the don't cares. That check is a tautology test on the cofactor of the other cubes with respect to the cube in question. Relatively essential primes are the cover-relative analogue of essential primes, but they are relative to the current cover, not to all primes.

## Redundant cubes and why they interact

A cube contained in the union of the others is **redundant**. Every cube is either relatively essential or redundant. Redundant cubes cannot all be removed at once: if cubes $A$ and $B$ cover the same leftover minterms, each is redundant while the other is present, but removing both uncovers those minterms. Espresso therefore splits the redundant cubes into totally redundant ones (covered by the relatively essential cubes and don't cares alone, safe to drop) and partially redundant ones (whose removal must be coordinated). In a cover of five primes where three are redundant, typically some are totally redundant and the rest compete for the same minterms.

## Minimum irredundant subcover

The partially redundant cubes and the minterms only they cover form a small covering problem: choose the fewest of them so that, with the relatively essential cubes, every ON minterm is covered. The result is an **irredundant cover**: no cube can be removed. For a cover of four primes such as `0--0`, `000-`, `1-11`, `11-1`, every cube turns out relatively essential and all four stay. Espresso solves this covering heuristically, since the subproblem is NP-hard in general but usually tiny. Prime plus irredundant is the local optimality Espresso guarantees: a cover can satisfy both properties and still not be minimum.

## Going deeper

Brayton et al., "Logic Minimization Algorithms for VLSI Synthesis" (1984), on IRREDUNDANT_COVER; Hachtel and Somenzi (1996), on heuristic two-level minimization.

label: The Espresso heuristic minimizer
lesson:
# The Espresso heuristic minimizer

Espresso, developed at IBM and Berkeley in the early 1980s, is the two-level minimizer that made PLA synthesis practical and still runs inside multi-level flows for node simplification. Instead of generating all primes, it improves a cover in place with expand, irredundant and reduce, using cube operations and tautology checks that scale to many inputs.

## The overall loop

Espresso first computes the OFF-set by complementing ON plus don't cares. It then runs EXPAND (make cubes prime, absorbing others) and IRREDUNDANT (drop unnecessary cubes), and extracts the essential primes, which it sets aside since they appear in every cover. The main loop repeats REDUCE, EXPAND, IRREDUNDANT while the cost (cubes, then literals) improves. When the loop stalls, LAST_GASP tries a different reduction to escape. The essentials are then added back. Every step preserves the function, so the result is always a valid cover; only its size is heuristic. The final cover is prime and irredundant, a local minimum.

## Why REDUCE helps

A prime and irredundant cover is stuck: expanding cannot grow its cubes further, and none can be removed. REDUCE makes progress possible by shrinking each cube, in order, to the smallest cube that still covers the minterms only it covers, given the rest of the cover. The reduced cover is no longer prime, but it represents the same function. The next EXPAND can now grow each cube in a different direction, possibly absorbing other cubes, and IRREDUNDANT may then remove more cubes. The sequence reduce, expand, irredundant moves the cover between local minima, and the order in which cubes are reduced matters as much as the expansion order.

## Scope and limits

Espresso handles multiple outputs by adding an output part to each cube, so that one product term can be shared by several outputs, exactly the row sharing a PLA rewards. It runs on cube lists with unate recursion, so functions with 30 or more inputs and thousands of cubes are routine. Its answer is not guaranteed minimum; Espresso-exact and later exact methods (based on implicit prime generation and covering) exist for small or structured functions. In multi-level synthesis Espresso, or an equivalent minimizer, simplifies the SOP of each network node using that node's don't cares, which is where it lives on in SIS-style flows.

## Going deeper

Brayton, Hachtel, McMullen and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Logic Minimization Algorithms for VLSI Synthesis" (1984); Rudell, "Logic Synthesis for VLSI Design", PhD thesis, UC Berkeley (1989).

label: Boolean networks
prereqs: Literal count, gate count and depth as cost
lesson:
# Boolean networks

Two-level forms are too large for most logic, so synthesis works on multi-level structure. The classic representation is the Boolean network: a directed acyclic graph whose internal nodes each hold a local Boolean function, usually as a sum of products, of their fanins. Every multi-level transformation of the MIS and SIS era, from factoring to don't-care simplification, is an operation on this graph.

## Nodes, edges and local functions

A Boolean network has primary inputs, primary outputs and internal nodes. Each internal node $y$ has a local function $y = f_y$ over its fanins, which may be primary inputs or other nodes, and an edge runs from each fanin to $y$. The graph is acyclic (registers cut cycles in sequential logic). For example, $x = a + b$, $y = c + f$, $z = xy + e$ is a three-node network computing $z = (a + b)(c + f) + e$. The global function of a node is obtained by substituting local functions recursively down to the primary inputs. Keeping local functions small and separate is the point: the network can share $x$ among many fanouts without duplicating it.

## Cost of a network

The usual area cost is the sum over nodes of the literals in each local function, counting a node name used as a fanin as one literal. For $x = a + b$ (2), $y = df + c$ (3), $z = ex + ey$ (4) and $w = fz + y$ (3) the total is 12 literals. Factored-form literals are a better area proxy than SOP literals, and SIS reports both. Delay is estimated by levels: primary inputs at level 0 and each node one more than its highest fanin, so in that example $x$ and $y$ are at level 1, $z$ at 2 and $w$ at 3. Both are computed in one topological pass and updated incrementally when a node changes.

## Transformations on the network

Multi-level optimization is a set of local moves on this graph. **Elimination** (collapsing) substitutes a node into its fanouts and deletes it, trading sharing for flatter logic. **Decomposition**, **extraction** and **substitution** create or reuse nodes for common divisors. **Simplification** minimizes a node's local SOP using don't cares derived from the rest of the network. Eliminating $x = bc + a$ into $z = ex + y$ gives $z = bce + ae + y$; here the total literal count happens to stay at 12, but in general elimination grows logic when the node has many fanouts. Every move must preserve the global functions at the outputs, and scripts alternate moves that grow and shrink the network.

## Going deeper

Brayton, Rudell, Sangiovanni-Vincentelli and Wang, "MIS: A multiple-level logic optimization system", IEEE TCAD (1987); Sentovich et al., "SIS: A system for sequential circuit synthesis", UC Berkeley memorandum UCB/ERL M92/41 (1992).

label: Weak division of SOP expressions
lesson:
# Weak division of SOP expressions

Multi-level synthesis finds structure by dividing expressions. Algebraic (weak) division treats an SOP as a polynomial: literals are variables, a complement is just another variable, and no Boolean identities are used. It is fast and predictable, and it is the engine behind kernels, factoring and extraction.

## Dividing by a cube

To divide an SOP $F$ by a single cube $c$, keep every cube of $F$ that contains all literals of $c$, and remove those literals from it. The result is the quotient $F/c$; the cubes not containing $c$ form the remainder. For $F = abg + ad + ae + af + bd + be + bf$ and $c = b$, the cubes containing $b$ are $abg$, $bd$, $be$, $bf$, so $F/b = ag + d + e + f$ with 4 cubes, and the remainder is $ad + ae + af$. Then $F = b(ag + d + e + f) + ad + ae + af$ exactly. Division by a cube is a filter and a strip, linear in the number of cubes.

## Dividing by a multi-cube divisor

For a divisor $D = d_1 + \dots + d_k$, compute each cube quotient $F/d_i$ and intersect them: $Q = \bigcap_i F/d_i$. The remainder is $R = F - DQ$, the cubes of $F$ not produced by multiplying $D$ and $Q$. For $F = ad + ae + af + bd + cd + ce + cf$ and $D = a + c$: $F/a = d + e + f$, $F/c = d + e + f$, so $Q = d + e + f$, $DQ$ accounts for six cubes, and $R = bd$ with 2 literals. If $F = bef + cef + bg + dh$ and $D = b + c$, then $F/b = ef + g$ and $F/c = ef$, so $Q = ef$, one cube. With sorted cube lists the whole division runs in $O(n \log n)$ time.

## What algebraic means

Weak division is exact as polynomial division: $F = DQ + R$ holds as an identity of polynomials, and $Q$ is the largest expression for which $DQ$ is contained in $F$. It is well defined only when $D$ and $Q$ have disjoint supports, so that multiplying them back creates no $x \cdot x$ or $x \cdot \bar{x}$ terms. The price is blindness to Boolean facts: $(a + b)(a + c) = a + bc$ is invisible, because it needs $a \cdot a = a$, and $\bar{a}$ is unrelated to $a$. The gain is speed and a clean theory of divisors (kernels). Boolean division recovers some of the lost cases using don't cares, at a much higher cost.

## Going deeper

Brayton and McMullen, "The decomposition and factorization of Boolean expressions", ISCAS (1982); De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), the chapter on multiple-level optimization.

label: Kernels and algebraic division
lesson:
# Kernels and algebraic division

Which divisors should synthesis try? Brayton and McMullen answered with kernels: the cube-free quotients of an expression by cubes. Kernels are few enough to enumerate, and every multiple-cube common divisor of two expressions shows up as an intersection of their kernels. They are the candidate set for factoring and for extracting shared logic.

## Cube-free quotients and kernels

An expression is **cube-free** if no single cube divides it evenly, that is, no literal appears in all its cubes (and it has at least two cubes). $ab + c$ is cube-free; $ab + ac = a(b + c)$ is not. A **kernel** of $F$ is a cube-free quotient $F/c$, and the cube $c$ is its **co-kernel**. $F$ itself is a kernel (with co-kernel 1) when it is cube-free. For $F = abd + adh + cf + e$: $F$ is cube-free, so it is a kernel, and $F/(ad) = b + h$ is another; no other cube gives a cube-free quotient of two or more cubes, so $F$ has 2 kernels.

## Enumerating kernels and co-kernels

Kernels are found recursively: for each literal appearing in at least two cubes, divide by it, make the quotient cube-free by dividing out the largest common cube, record the kernel, and recurse on it, skipping literals already handled to avoid repeats. Several co-kernels can give the same kernel. For $F = bcdf + bcef + cdfg + cefg = cf(b + g)(d + e)$: dividing by $cf$ gives $bd + be + dg + eg$; by $bcf$ or $cfg$ gives $d + e$; by $cdf$ or $cef$ gives $b + g$. That is 3 distinct kernels and 5 co-kernels. $F$ itself is not a kernel, since $cf$ divides every cube.

## Levels and the intersection theorem

A kernel is **level 0** if it has no kernels other than itself; a level-$n$ kernel has kernels of level at most $n - 1$, with at least one of level $n - 1$. For $F = af + bc + cf + e$ the kernels are $F$, $a + c$ (co-kernel $f$) and $b + f$ (co-kernel $c$); the last two are level 0. Level-0 kernels are cheap to compute and often enough in practice. The key theorem: two expressions $F$ and $G$ have a common divisor of more than one cube if and only if some kernel of $F$ and some kernel of $G$ intersect in more than one cube. So searching kernel intersections finds every multiple-cube common divisor, which is how kernel extraction decides what to share.

## Going deeper

Brayton and McMullen, "The decomposition and factorization of Boolean expressions", ISCAS (1982); Brayton, Hachtel and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Multilevel logic synthesis", Proceedings of the IEEE (1990).

label: Factored forms and literal counts
lesson:
# Factored forms and literal counts

A factored form is a parenthesized expression of sums and products, such as $(a + b)(c + d) + e$. It is the multi-level analogue of an SOP and the best simple model of a static CMOS complex gate, since each literal becomes a transistor pair. Converting between factored forms and SOPs, and counting literals of each, is the core arithmetic of multi-level area estimation.

## Expanding a factored form

Multiplying a factored form out gives an SOP. Cube counts follow simple rules: a sum adds the cube counts of its terms, and a product multiplies them. For $F = (c(e + bg) + h)d$: the inner $e + bg$ has 2 cubes, times $c$ still 2, plus $h$ makes 3, times $d$ stays 3. So the SOP $cde + bcdg + dh$ has 3 cubes. When every variable appears once (a read-once form), there is no simplification during expansion, so these rules are exact. With repeated variables, expansion can produce duplicate or absorbed cubes and the counts become upper bounds.

## SOP literals from a factored form

Literals multiply too. For a product $AB$ the SOP literal count is $l_A c_B + l_B c_A$, where $c$ is a cube count and $l$ a literal count, because each literal of $A$ appears once with every cube of $B$. For a sum, literals add. For $F = ga(h + b + f + ed)$: $ga$ has 1 cube and 2 literals, $h + b + f + ed$ has 4 cubes and 5 literals, so the SOP has $2 \cdot 4 + 5 \cdot 1 = 13$ literals: $agh + abg + afg + adeg$. The factored form has 6. The gap grows quickly with nesting, which is why SOP literal count overstates the area of multi-level logic.

## Finding a good factored form

The literal count of a factored form is the number of leaves. Finding the minimum-literal factored form is hard, so tools use heuristics. **Quick factor** divides $F$ by a level-0 kernel $K$, giving $F = KQ + R$, and recursively factors $K$, $Q$ and $R$. **Good factor** chooses the kernel that saves the most literals. For $bceg + bceh + ad$ (10 literals), dividing by the kernel $g + h$ gives $bce(g + h) + ad$ with 7 literals, a saving of 3. Read-once functions are the easy case, with one leaf per variable, which is optimal. Factored-form literal count is SIS's default area cost and the basis of refactoring in ABC.

## Going deeper

Brayton, "Factoring logic functions", IBM Journal of Research and Development (1987); Hachtel and Somenzi, "Logic Synthesis and Verification Algorithms" (1996), on multi-level factoring.

label: Extracting common kernels
lesson:
# Extracting common kernels

Extraction finds a divisor shared by several functions, creates one node for it, and rewrites each function to use that node. It is the multi-level move that saves the most area, because logic computed once is reused many times. Kernel extraction (the gkx command in SIS) is the multi-cube version; its literal accounting decides whether a candidate is worth extracting.

## Literals before extraction

Start from the SOPs of the functions that share a divisor. For $F_1 = bcde + ade + g$ and $F_2 = bcd + ad + g$ the common divisor is $D = bc + a$: $F_1 = (bc + a)de + g$ and $F_2 = (bc + a)d + g$. Before extraction the literal count is simply the sum over all cubes: $4 + 3 + 1 = 8$ for $F_1$ and $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$ for $F_2$, 14 in total. The kernels of $F_1$ include $bc + a$ (co-kernel $de$) and those of $F_2$ include $bc + a$ (co-kernel $d$); their intersection is the two-cube divisor $D$.

## Literals after extraction

Create the node $X = D$ and rewrite each function as $XQ + R$, where $Q$ and $R$ come from weak division by $D$. Count the literals of $X$ once, then for each function count each quotient cube's literals plus one for the literal $X$, plus the remainder's literals. For the example: $X = bc + a$ costs 3. $F_1 = Xde + g$ costs $(2 + 1) + 1 = 4$ and $F_2 = Xd + g$ costs $(1 + 1) + 1 = 3$. Total $3 + 4 + 3 = 10$. A quotient of the single cube 1 still costs one literal, the $X$ itself: $F = D + h$ becomes $X + h$ with 2 literals.

## Value, greed and the extraction loop

The value of extracting $D$ is literals before minus literals after: 14 - 10 = 4 in the example. Kernel extraction repeatedly picks the divisor of highest value among kernel intersections, extracts it, and updates the network, until no divisor saves literals. The search can be cast as rectangle covering on a co-kernel/cube matrix, where a rectangle is a set of co-kernels sharing a set of kernel cubes. Fast extract (fx), used in SIS and ABC, restricts candidates to double-cube divisors and single-cube divisors, which can be enumerated and updated incrementally on very large networks. Extraction increases fanout, so a later stage may need to buffer or duplicate the shared node.

## Going deeper

Rajski and Vasudevamurthy, "The testability-preserving concurrent decomposition and factorization of Boolean expressions", IEEE TCAD (1992), which introduced fast extraction; Brayton, Rudell, Sangiovanni-Vincentelli and Wang, "MIS", IEEE TCAD (1987).

label: Single-cube extraction
lesson:
# Single-cube extraction

The simplest shared divisor is a single cube, such as $ab$ appearing inside many product terms. Extracting it as a new node trades several copies of its literals for one node and one literal per use. The value formula is short, and it shows exactly when sharing pays: often enough to use, never so often that extraction is free.

## Counting occurrences

A cube $c$ divides a cube $q$ when every literal of $c$ appears in $q$. Count how many cubes across all functions contain $c$; call it $m$. In $F_1 = aef + bce + def$ and $F_2 = abcf + abdf + aef + be$, the cube $df$ divides $def$ and $abdf$, so $m = 2$. The same count over all pairs of literals, kept in a matrix of cube-literal incidences, is how single-cube extraction finds candidates. Cubes of $m = 1$ are useless for sharing, since a node used once saves nothing; the interesting candidates divide two or more cubes, possibly in different functions.

## Literals after extracting a cube

Create $X = c$ with $k$ literals and replace $c$ by $X$ in each of the $m$ cubes it divides. Each such cube loses $k$ literals and gains one, and $X$ itself adds $k$. The new total is $L - mk + m + k$. For $F_1 = abd + cde + cdf$ and $F_2 = ae + af + bd + cd$, extracting $X = bd$ ($k = 2$, $m = 2$, $L = 17$) gives $17 - 4 + 2 + 2 = 17$: no gain. Extracting $X = cd$ instead ($k = 2$, $m = 3$) gives $17 - 6 + 3 + 2 = 16$. The new node also adds a level of logic to each use, which is the delay cost of sharing.

## The value formula

The saving is $mk - m - k = (m - 1)(k - 1) - 1$. It is positive only when $m \ge 2$, $k \ge 2$ and not both equal 2: a two-literal cube used twice saves nothing, used three times saves 1, and a three-literal cube used three times saves 3. For $F_1 = abcf + cd + ce$ and $F_2 = abde + bcef + abf$, a best candidate is $ab$, used 3 times, saving $3 \cdot 2 - 3 - 2 = 1$ (the cube $abf$, used twice, ties with $2 \cdot 3 - 2 - 3 = 1$). Greedy extraction picks the best value, updates the counts and repeats. The formula assumes literal count is area; with a real library a node also costs a gate and an extra level, so tools require a margin.

## Going deeper

Rajski and Vasudevamurthy, IEEE TCAD (1992), on single-cube and double-cube extraction; Rudell, "Logic Synthesis for VLSI Design", PhD thesis, UC Berkeley (1989), on rectangle covering.

label: Node elimination and its literal value
lesson:
# Node elimination and its literal value

Elimination removes a node by substituting its function into every fanout. It undoes sharing, which sounds wasteful, but it exposes optimization across node boundaries: after collapsing, a larger node can be re-minimized and re-factored. SIS-style scripts eliminate nodes whose removal costs few literals, then re-extract. The value of a node decides which ones go.

## The value of a node

Suppose node $t$ has a factored form with $l$ literals and appears as a single literal in $n$ fanout expressions. Eliminating it replaces each use by a copy of the factored form, so the network gains $nl$ literals and loses the $l$ literals of $t$ plus the $n$ uses: the change is $nl - n - l = (n - 1)(l - 1) - 1$. A node with $l = 3$ and $n = 5$ has value $15 - 8 = 7$. A node used once has value -1: eliminating it always saves the literal of its use. This is the mirror image of the extraction saving, which is why extraction and elimination are paired in scripts.

## Threshold elimination

The SIS command eliminate with a threshold $T$ collapses every node whose value is at most $T$. A threshold of -1 removes only nodes used once; a threshold of 0 or more also removes small shared nodes; large thresholds collapse almost everything. Given candidates $t_1$ (2 literals, 1 use, value -1), $t_2$ (4 literals, 1 use, value -1), $t_3$ (3 literals, 2 uses, value 1), $t_4$ (4 literals, 2 uses, value 2), a threshold of 1 eliminates $t_1$, $t_2$ and $t_3$. Values change as nodes are eliminated, since collapsing one node can change the literal counts and use counts of others, so the pass recomputes them as it goes.

## Exact change in SOP literals

In SOP terms elimination multiplies out. If $x$ has $c$ cubes and $L$ literals and appears in a fanout cube $qx$ where $q$ has $l_q$ literals, that cube becomes $c$ cubes with $l_q c + L$ literals in total. For $x = ac + bc$ ($c = 2$, $L = 4$) used in $ex$, $gx$ and $dgx$: before, $4 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 11$ literals; after, $(2 + 4) + (2 + 4) + (4 + 4) = 20$. The change is $+9$. SOP literal growth is larger than factored growth because multiplying out loses the factoring. Collapsing is the first step of refactoring and of node simplification with don't cares, so a temporary increase is often accepted.

## Going deeper

Sentovich et al., "SIS: A system for sequential circuit synthesis", UCB/ERL M92/41 (1992), on eliminate and the standard scripts; De Micheli (1994), the chapter on multiple-level optimization.

label: Boolean versus algebraic division
prereqs: Logical equivalence, De Morgan and normal forms
lesson:
# Boolean versus algebraic division

Algebraic division is fast but treats a and its complement as unrelated and never uses $x \cdot x = x$. Boolean division can use any identity and any don't care, at much higher cost. Knowing what each can see tells a tool designer when cheap algebraic passes suffice and when a Boolean pass, such as resubstitution with don't cares, is worth its run time.

## What algebraic methods miss

Algebraic division works on SOPs as polynomials, so three classes of rewrite are invisible. Idempotence: $(a + b)(a + c) = a + bc$ needs $a \cdot a = a$. Complements: $a + \bar{a}b = a + b$ needs $a + \bar{a} = 1$. Absorption: $a + ab = a$. Purely algebraic identities, such as $ac + ad + bc + bd = (a + b)(c + d)$, are found. A useful test: if verifying the identity requires treating literals as Boolean rather than as independent polynomial variables, weak division cannot find it. Every algebraic factorization is Boolean-valid, so Boolean methods find a superset of the factorizations.

## Boolean division with don't cares

To divide $f$ by $g$ in a Boolean way, introduce a new variable $y$ standing for $g$, with the don't care $y \oplus g$ (points where $y$ and $g$ disagree never occur). Then minimize $f$ as a function of its inputs and $y$, using that don't care. The minimizer may rewrite $f$ in terms of $y$ wherever that is cheaper. For $f = a + bc$ and an existing node $g = a + b$, algebraic division fails ($f/a = 1$ and $f/b = c$ have an empty intersection), but Boolean minimization finds $f = y(a + c)$, which is correct because $(a + b)(a + c) = a + bc$.

## When to pay for Boolean methods

Algebraic methods run in near-linear time per division and scale to whole networks, so they are used for global restructuring. Boolean methods need don't-care computation and minimization or SAT, so they are applied locally: resubstitution tries a few divisors near each node, inside a window. Some structure only Boolean methods can see, for example multiplexer and XOR forms written in SOP, where $a$ and $\bar{a}$ appear in different cubes. For read-once functions algebraic factoring is already optimal. Modern AIG flows mostly replace algebraic passes with rewriting and truth-table based resubstitution, which are Boolean by construction but local.

## Going deeper

Brayton, Hachtel and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Multilevel logic synthesis", Proceedings of the IEEE (1990); Hachtel and Somenzi (1996), on Boolean division.

label: Don't-care conditions
lesson:
# Don't-care conditions

A don't care is a point where the circuit's value does not matter, and every don't care is freedom to simplify. Some come from the specification (external don't cares); others arise inside a network because some value combinations can never occur or can never be observed. Understanding where don't cares come from and when using them is safe is central to node simplification and resubstitution.

## External don't cares

External don't cares are given by the environment. A BCD decoder never sees input codes 10 to 15, so its outputs on those codes are free. A five-state FSM encoded in three bits has three unused codes, which are don't cares for the next-state and output logic if the machine can never reach them. An output that is ignored under some condition (a valid bit is low) is a don't care on those inputs. In a K-map these cells may join any group or none. The risk: a don't care is a promise. If the impossible input does occur, after a soft error in an FSM for instance, the circuit outputs whatever the minimizer chose.

## Don't cares inside a network

Inside a Boolean network two more kinds appear. **Satisfiability don't cares**: for a node $y = f(x)$, combinations where $y \ne f(x)$ can never happen, so the set $y \oplus f(x)$ is a don't care for any node that sees both $y$ and $x$. If $y = ab$ feeds $z$ alongside $a$, then $y = 1$ with $a = 0$ never occurs. **Observability don't cares**: an input of a node is unobservable when the outputs do not depend on it; for $z = y + c$, the value of $y$ does not matter whenever $c = 1$. Formally the ODC of $y$ with respect to $z$ is the complement of the Boolean difference $z|_{y=1} \oplus z|_{y=0}$.

## Using don't cares safely

A node may be replaced by any function that agrees with it wherever the node is both controllable (its local input pattern can occur) and observable (its value can reach an output). Inside that care set it must match; outside it is free. Exact global don't cares can be huge, so tools compute them over a window of nearby logic, by BDDs on small windows or by simulation and SAT. Two cautions: don't cares of different nodes interact, so using full ODCs at several nodes at once can be wrong; and removing logic covered by don't cares also removes redundancy that would make stuck-at faults untestable, which is why don't-care optimization improves testability.

## Going deeper

Bartlett et al., "Multilevel logic minimization using implicit don't cares", IEEE TCAD (1988); Savoj and Brayton, "The use of observability and external don't cares for the simplification of multi-level networks", DAC (1990).

problems.q:
Which kind of don't care comes from the design's environment rather than from its internal structure?

A) Satisfiability don't cares

B) Observability don't cares

C) External don't cares

D) Controllability don't cares of an internal node
problems.a: External don't cares
problems.e: External don't cares are given by the specification (impossible inputs, ignored outputs); the others are derived from the network itself.

D) Nothing, unused codes must be treated as 0
problems.a: Don't cares, provided the machine can never reach those codes
problems.e: Unreachable state codes are external don't cares for the next-state and output logic, though safety-critical designs may still define them.
